prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new precision tests of nature

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the lattice clock second, but after reading the other seven ballots I now put B057 first. It is the only shortlisted candidate that all eight members ranked, five of them in their top three, and all eight proposed the identical pair, Katori and Ye. That is not merit by itself, so I tested it against my own criteria. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the Doppler and recoil problem and lets many atoms be interrogated at once, and the gain is a measured one, from about 1e-15 to about 1e-18, not a promised one. Independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, SYRTE, PTB and others) reproduce and intercompare the clocks, which is the test I apply to any instrument result, and systematics control is the whole point of the achievement. The payoffs are concrete: relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the candidate redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori the concept and first demonstration, Ye the performance frontier and the many-body clock. I would frame the citation around the lattice clock as a measurement instrument, so it does not reach into the comb (2005) or ion-trap (2012) territory.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this could be read as an incremental continuation of the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (trapped single quantum systems) prizes in precision optical metrology, and that the decisive credit is spread across Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and others who are not named. A second reservation is Mehlig's: the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the societal payoff is still ahead of us and a prize could wait. Against that, a Nobel Prize rewards the demonstrated measurement advance, not its later standardisation, and the three-person limit makes a two-name pair a fair, if imperfect, reading of the historical record. I also accept that a lattice clock prize says nothing about the condensed-matter and quantum-material frontier that three colleagues put first, and the committee should be honest that this is a choice between breadth of agreement and perceived novelty.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B057 first because it is measurement-limited progress: 1e-18 uncertainty, many reproducing groups, and a clean two-person credit, with the main risk being whether to credit a broader set of clock pioneers.
responses.response: I agree with the criterion and the conclusion, and it is close to my own test of independent reproduction and control of systematics. On the broader-pioneers concern I would not widen the credit: the three-person rule and the Katori-Ye split are cleaner than for any other candidate, and the Lemonde, Gill and NIST contributions are real but follow-on. I do differ with you on B035 as a close second. Atom interferometry has a strong case, but the allocation among Borde, Pritchard, Kasevich and Muller is contested even between you and Lindroth, who both leave out Muller, whereas B057 has no such tension.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B057 only seventh and notes that it may be better timed after the redefinition of the SI second, besides overlapping with the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously, but I do not find it persuasive. The prize is for the demonstrated 1e-18 clock, which exists today and has been confirmed in international comparisons, and the redefinition is a metrological-body decision that follows the physics rather than defines it. Waiting would also repeat the pattern of delaying a mature discovery. On overlap, the 2005 prize was for the comb as the frequency ruler and 2012 for single trapped quantum systems; the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice and its quantum-limited operation are a distinct step. Where I do concede ground is B015: your argument that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is a simple mechanism with broad consequences is a strong one, and I lean on you for the condensed-matter detail.

responses.point: Olsson puts twisted bilayer graphene first for opening a new experimental platform, ranks topological insulators second and the lattice clock third, and also ranks IceCube sixth with doubts about the roles of AMANDA and Baikal and source identification.
responses.response: On B054 you are right on the facts and I have revised my view accordingly: source identification rests on a handful of objects at roughly 3 to 4 sigma, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are only beginning to confirm, and the allocation among Halzen, Karle and Spiering with the AMANDA lineage is not obviously unique. That is why I am keeping IceCube as an alternative and not as my preferred prize. On B015 I accept it is a leading candidate, but your own uncertainty about whether the field is old enough, and the still-disputed pairing mechanism, are what hold me back from putting it first. I would be content with it if the committee wanted to recognise the correlated-matter platform, provided the citation avoids claiming a settled mechanism.

responses.point: Eriksson places twisted bilayer graphene first and topological insulators second, and ranks the lattice clock only eighth, while saying clocks lie outside his core area and deferring to atomic-physics colleagues.
responses.response: I respect the deference and I will apply the same rule to myself on B015 and B053, where I am relying on you and on Mehlig. The point I would ask you to weigh is that B057 is the one candidate on which the two atomic-physics members (Lindroth and Kroll), who have the most direct expertise, both put it first. For the condensed-matter candidates the disagreement is within the field: you and Danielsson differ on whether Mele or Hasan should be credited with Kane and Molenkamp, and four members put B053 in their top three yet no two of them propose the same trio. That unsettled allocation, not the science, is the main reason I do not push B053.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on conceptual clarity but flags that a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 is a balance question and that Girvin and Devoret are missing from the credit.
responses.response: I share your two reservations on B021. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and recognising a related circuit architecture a year later would make the committee's choices look clustered, while leaving out Girvin and Devoret makes the credit incomplete. I also note you ranked B057 third and found its credit reasonably clean, so you and I agree on that. I disagree that circuit QED should lead: its ranking spread is wide, from your first place to Lindroth's eighth, and I do not see the case for taking it ahead of a candidate with a flat, widely shared ranking.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct achievement or as an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes
Whether the credit should be limited to Katori and Ye or whether other lattice-clock pioneers (Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow) have claims that change the framing
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the SI second before awarding it

The condensed-matter candidates (B015, B053) are outside my expertise, so I cannot independently judge the maturity of the superconducting mechanism in magic-angle graphene or the Hasan-versus-Mele allocation
Whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a second achievement would serve the committee better than a single award
statement.conflict_note: I have no specific conflict with B057, B015, B053 or the atomic-physics and quantum-optics candidates from my profile. My own field is astroparticle physics, which is adjacent to B054 (IceCube) but I have no collaboration or institutional tie to IceCube (my collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur), so no recusal is needed, though colleagues should weigh my ranking of B054 knowing my field.
